prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: In my opening I ranked B040 first and B009 second. After reading the colleagues' arguments, I now prefer B009 as the single configuration. Two strands converge here. One is the skill-biased and task-based account of labour demand (Katz, Autor). The other is the quasi-experimental trade-shock evidence on local labour markets (Autor, Hanson). Together they explain wage polarisation, adjustment costs and persistent regional effects. The work uses transparent designs and has been replicated in many countries over more than a decade. The evidence base is mature, since the main papers run from the early 1990s to the mid-2010s. It has also shaped policy and public understanding of technology and globalisation, which is a concrete benefit to society. Compared with B040, the identification is more credible, because B040 relies partly on cross-country constitutional comparisons. B009's overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes is a matter of framing. B040's thematic overlap with the 2024 institutions prize is arguably closer. The credit is concentrated enough to support three named laureates without being arbitrary.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. The three-name limit excludes David Dorn, a core co-author of the China-shock papers, and omits Levy and Murnane from the task framework. The task-based theoretical core is also associated with Acemoglu and Restrepo, and the 2023 (Goldin) and 2024 (Acemoglu) prizes touch adjacent ground. The citation must therefore be drafted carefully so it credits the empirical and conceptual contribution of these three without implying priority over work already recognised. The magnitude and persistence of the shift-share trade-shock estimates remain debated. A committee could reasonably see two separable discoveries (technology and trade) that do not belong in one prize.

responses.point: Teorell proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn, centred on the China shock, and treats Katz and the skill-premium work as a parallel contribution whose credit boundary is contestable.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously. Dorn is as central to the trade-shock papers as Hanson. I still prefer Autor, Hanson and Katz, because that citation covers both strands. Autor appears in both. Katz is the foundation of the supply-demand-and-technology account of the skill premium, and it is older and better confirmed than the trade-shock magnitudes. A Dorn-based trio would narrow the prize to a trade-exposure result whose persistence and size are still debated. I would not call my choice clearly superior, and if the committee prefers the trade-shock framing, Dorn in place of Katz is a defensible variant.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B009 third and flags that the task framework's theoretical core is tied to Acemoglu and Restrepo, so the 2024 prize complicates attribution. He also notes the uncertainty about choosing three of four names.
responses.response: I agree this is the main attribution risk, and it is why I would write the citation around labour-demand evidence on technology and trade rather than a theory of automation. The empirical task-polarisation and trade-shock results in Autor, Katz and Hanson are separate from the directed-technology theory honoured in 2024, though they are related. I do not think the overlap disqualifies B009. The committee should record it explicitly, and I would be cautious about any citation wording that claims the task framework as theory.

responses.point: Fredriksson places B009 first for its replicated findings, transparent identification and policy relevance. He also flags the 2024 and 2023 overlap and the shift-share persistence debate, and he ranks B040 fourth, noting overlap with the 2024 institutions prize and weaker identification of cross-country constitutional findings.
responses.response: I agree with both halves, and this is what moved me. My opening placed B040 first because of its concentrated attribution. Fredriksson's point about identification in the constitutional work, and the closer thematic overlap with the 2024 prize, weigh more with me now. I would still keep B040 as an alternative, because its three-person core is cleaner than B009's. On the shift-share critique, I think the core results hold up, but I do not want to understate that magnitudes and external validity outside the United States are open questions.

uncertainties: Whether Dorn should replace Katz, or whether the committee would prefer a narrower trade-shock prize.
How much the 2023 (Goldin) and 2024 (Acemoglu) prizes already cover the labour-demand and technology territory, and how a citation can delimit it.
The persistence and external validity of the China-shock estimates, including the shift-share inference debate.
Whether the technology and trade strands are one achievement or two, and whether a two-part configuration is warranted. Within the three-person limit it would force an unattractive split of credit.
Katz also appears in B050, and the committee has not settled how credit should be divided between the two entries.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the B009 candidates. My documented connections are co-authorship and IIES ties with committee colleagues (Krusell, Boppart, Friberg), none of whom is a credited name on the shortlist. In my opening I flagged a possible Stockholm proximity of some B040 candidates. The supplied profile does not document that connection, so it is an unverified general-knowledge concern, disclosed and not adjudicated. B040 is now only an alternative.
